# Mine

Mine is a set of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) to digitalize ones personal or professional life.
The key idea is to save everything in a repo as markdown files. This can be calendar entries,
diaries, markdowns extracted from voice recordings / pdfs / .. These .md files can easily be
ported to new apps without a vendor lock-in and are processed via an (AI) assistant to help you
plan your day, keep track of tasks, remind you of memories a.k.a. a second brain.

To keep complexity to a minimum each use-case lives in a separate folder. e.g. the calendar PWA
lives completely in a 'calendar' folder as does the zettelkasten and all the other apps. Each
folder contains a 'sample' folder with samples how the markdowns shall look, a REQUIREMENTS.md
describing how the PWA works and a TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md describing how it is built.

See [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how this is built, and
[TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md) for how it is checked.

## One app, one setup

Mine installs as **one** app on the phone, with one icon. The apps in the subfolders are pages
inside it, not separate installs.

This is what makes the central requirement work: **the GitHub repo and token are entered once,
in the main app, and every app in a subfolder uses them.** Verified on iPhone and Android.

## Main app

A tile per app: its `icon.svg` above its folder name.

Above the tiles, apps may contribute a summary. The calendar's shows today's entries and the
next one — which matters, because opening the app is the only reminder that works (see below).

## First run

1. Open the app URL and add it to the home screen (iOS: Share → Add to Home Screen;
   Android: menu → Install).
2. The setup screen asks for GitHub owner, data repo, branch, and a personal access token.
3. The app tests the connection and reports clearly if it fails.

Settings are stored on the device only. The token is never displayed again after entry, and the
app warns 14 days before it expires.

# Mine — technical requirements

How [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) is built. Everything here was verified against the live
API or on device on 2026-11-19; `spike/` re-runs the device checks and needs no token.

## Repos
**Load with `CORE_SCHEMA`, never js-yaml's default.** The default is YAML 1.1 and parses
`start: 2026-04-18` into a JS Date at UTC midnight — silently shifting every all-day entry by a
day east of UTC. `CORE_SCHEMA` keeps it a string and still handles bools, numbers, flow maps and
quoted scalars. This is the same off-by-one the bare-date format exists to prevent, arriving
through the parser instead.

## Platform findings

Verified in both installed home-screen apps (iPhone/Safari, Pixel/Chrome) on 2026-11-19.

| | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Storage shared across paths | **Yes.** A marker written by `/mine/spike/` was read back byte-identical by `/mine/spike/sub/`, both reporting `STANDALONE`. Cross-path module imports work too. |
| `{type:'module'}` service worker | Registers on Safari as well as Chrome. No classic fallback needed. |
| `storage.persisted()` | **Already granted**, no prompt, on both. An installed app is exempt from the ~7-day eviction that applies to uninstalled sites, so the token and mirror survive idle periods. |
| Quota | 35 GB (iPhone), 56 GB (Pixel), against a mirror measured in single-digit MB. |

Not tested, and no longer relevant: whether separately-installed PWAs get isolated storage. That
expectation is why the one-app topology was chosen.

Re-run `spike/` after a major iOS release — two of the four results above contradicted the
documented platform behaviour, and that is exactly the kind of thing that regresses silently.

- **the real device** — a system font scale, a notch, a software keyboard, Safari's and
  Chrome's own quirks. Serve the tree with `python3 -m http.server` and open it from the phone

- **GitHub sync**: pulling, the one-commit drain, conflict files, an expiring token. Only a real

# Calendar

Calendar is an app of [Mine](../REQUIREMENTS.md) to manage your calendar. Every entry is one
markdown file in the data repo, so your calendar stays readable and portable without this app.

See [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) for the file format.

## What an entry holds

A title, a type — **event** or **task** — a start and end, a group, a location, participants,
alerts, and a free markdown body for the agenda, checklist or notes.

A task also carries a **stage** — `todo`, `doing` or `done`. An event has none, and stage is the
only record of a task's progress; there is no separate done flag.

**Important is not a task's alone.** An event can be marked too, because the thing a filter
narrows a view down to is what matters, and in a calendar half of what matters is a meeting. It
is the one of the three task fields that was never about progress.

**Important is a plain yes or no, not a scale.** There is no priority 1, 2 and 3. Three tiers
asked you to decide twice — once whether an entry matters and again how much — and the second
answer never changed what got done first. An entry that matters carries `important: true`; one
that does not carries no key at all.

A new task starts at `todo`, which is a default and nothing more: it can be changed before
saving.

**There is no estimate.** A task used to carry one, in days, and nothing ever read it: it was
shown in the popup that set it and nowhere else, so it was a number to keep up to date rather
than one to act on. The field, its hourglass and its default of one day are gone. A file that
still carries an `estimate` key keeps it — the form does not own that key any more, so it
survives a save the way any hand-added key does.

Entries can repeat, and a repeating entry can have single occurrences skipped, moved, retitled
or moved to another stage without affecting the rest.

## Layout

A navigation pane at the top and a big calendar window below it.

**The calendar window is as wide as the browser.** Nothing caps it: a month at 1920 px is a
month 1920 px wide, because the one thing a desktop has over a phone is room, and a grid that
stops at 78 rem spends that room on margins. **The board is the exception** and keeps the cap,
centred — three columns stretched across a wide monitor are three columns of mostly empty card,
and a card is read at the width a sentence is read at, not at a third of the screen. The pane
itself is full width in both, so it never changes shape when you switch between them.

In the top pane, three groups: the two view controls and the search at the left, the period in
the middle, the filter, the hamburger and the way out at the right.

```
[board]    [M]  [search]     [‹]   [NOV/26]   [›]     [filter] [☰] [⌂]     a calendar view
[calendar] [▥]  [search]     [‹]   [7]        [›]     [filter] [☰] [⌂]     the kanban
```

Everything in the pane is drawn at **twice the size** it was: this is the row reached for on
every visit, and it was the smallest thing on the screen.

**On a phone the pane is two rows**, each one filling the width:

```
[board] [M] [search] [filter] [☰] [⌂]     the six that go somewhere
[‹]        [ NOV/26 ]        [›]          the period, and the way to another
```

Five controls across one line left the period label — the one thing in the pane you read rather
than aim at — no wider than the buttons beside it, and the arrows that step it had to be dropped
to make even that fit. A second row buys back both. **The six controls that go somewhere share
the first row equally**, three from each side, so neither side's buttons are wider than the
other's; the period takes the second, where **the two arrows are equal in size
and the label between them is larger**, because the label carries a date to be read and an arrow
carries only a direction. The pane still fits a 320 px viewport, and neither row drops a control
or lets one wrap away.

- **Leftmost, the view switch and the zoom.** One slot always holds the way to the other kind
  of view: a board icon in a calendar view, and on the board a calendar icon, which returns to
  the month view. The board is not a zoom step, which is why it has a slot of its own rather
  than a place in the zoom's list. Beside it the **zoom**, which shows the view you are in —
  described below — and then the **search**, a magnifier, described under *Search*.
- **Centred, the period.** Left/right buttons, with the period label between them, to move to
  the previous/next day, week, month, year or sprint, depending on the current view. The label
  is short, because the pane has to fit a phone:

  | view | label |
  | --- | --- |
  | day | `FR 20/NOV` |
  | week | `W47/NOV` |
  | month | `NOV/26` |
  | year | `2026` |
  | kanban | `7` — the sprint number alone |

  The month name is the device locale's three-letter abbreviation, upper-cased, so a German
  phone reads `OKT/26`: short beats English. The week label always carries its ISO week number,
  whether or not *show calendar weeks* is on — that setting governs the month view's gutter and
  nothing else. A week spanning two months takes the month its **fourth** day is in, which is
  the rule the gutter already uses, so label and gutter can never disagree.

  **Clicking the label opens the picker**, and that is the only thing it does — in every view
  and on a phone as much as on a desktop. **There is no caret `▾`.** The caret existed only
  because the label's own tap was taken by the zoom; the zoom is a button of its own now, so the
  label is free to be the one thing it was always read as — the period, pressed to pick another.
  This is also what the board has always done, so the two kinds of view no longer differ in what
  their label means. The label carries no glyph saying it is pressable: it takes a hover and a
  press background, as the year view's month caption does.

  The picker shows a month at a time, with its name top left and left/right arrows top right.
  Clicking the month name switches to a year grid of 9 years ending with the current one, whose
  arrows page by 9 years. Today is highlighted in it, and tapping it is how you get back to today
  — there is no jump-to-today button in the pane. In the kanban the picker picks a sprint: its
  rows read `Sprint 7 · 19 Jan – 1 Feb`, and the row holding today reads
  `current · 19 Jan – 1 Feb` on a brighter background in dark mode, a darker one in light.

  **The two arrows stand well clear of the label.** On a desktop the gap either side of it is
  about half an arrow — three controls crammed together read as one control, and this is the
  group the pane is used through. On a phone the second row keeps its tight gap, because there
  the arrows are flexible halves and every millimetre of gap is taken off a thumb's target.

  **On a phone the `‹` `›` are on the second row, drawn at the size of the first row's icons.**
  They were larger than everything above them, which made the row that steps the period louder
  than the four that leave it. And **there is no swipe anywhere in the calendar**: the label was
  swiped only because the arrows were not there to press; now that they have a row of their own
  they are, and a gesture doing what a visible button does is the same second mechanism this
  document refuses a card on a desktop. So no sideways gesture does anything, in any view, and
  nothing ever has to be told apart from a card drag on the board or from a scroll in a grid.
- **Rightmost, the filter and the two ways out.** A **filter** button, a funnel, that opens the
  filter directly; a **hamburger** button that names its two errands — `settings` and `logs` —
  and opens whichever is tapped; and a home icon back to the Mine tile screen. A house rather than an arrow, because a third arrow beside the two that step through
  periods reads as another way to move inside the calendar.

### Moving the pane to the bottom

**The pane can be dragged to the bottom of the screen, and back.** Pressing anywhere on it for a
moment — a button included, with a finger or a mouse — lifts the whole pane, both rows on a
phone; two dashed places appear at the top and the bottom of the screen, the one in whose half
the pane is held is marked, and releasing docks it there. A press that does not hold is still a
click on whatever was pressed, and a hold opens nothing. Where it is docked is **remembered per
device**, like the board's orientation, and holds for every view, the board included.

At the bottom, **the sync line moves to the top**, so the two never stack, and **on a phone the
two rows swap**: the period goes on the upper row and the six buttons on the lower, nearest the
## The filter, the settings and the logs

**The filter has a button of its own.** It is the overlay you open daily, and a menu in front
of it spent a tap naming the one errand you came for. Its funnel sits at the right of the pane,
beside the hamburger.

**The hamburger holds the other two, named before either opens.** It opens a short dropdown
reading `settings` and `logs`, and opens neither; a second tap opens the one that was meant.

They were one panel for a while, under a heading each. A heading is a weak way to separate a thing
you open daily from a thing you open twice, and it cost the filter the room to show its groups:
the list had to be folded away or it pushed the nine settings rows below the fold. Naming the two
and opening them apart costs one tap and buys each of them its own shape.

**The filter is a dropdown off its button.** It is the overlay you open often — a group hidden
this afternoon, the board narrowed to what is important — and the view it narrows has to stay in
sight while it is narrowed, which a centred card over the middle of the screen cannot do.

**The settings are a centred panel**, titled `Settings`, whose top right has an `x` to close.
They are the nine rows that change once, so they may take the middle of the screen.

**The logs are a centred panel too**, titled `Logs`, and they are the answer to a sync line that
says something unexpected. The line `14 change(s) pending` used to be the whole of what the app
would say about a queue that could not drain: the reason was written to that same line by
whichever push failed and overwritten by the next focus, so a browser could sit on a count it
could neither explain nor clear. The panel holds three things —

- **the state**, with `push now` and `discard all` beside it;
- **the last attempt**: whether it was a push or a pull, what it failed with, how many times in a
  row, and since when;
- **what is waiting**: one line per queued change — `put` or `del`, its path, and how long it has
  been there.

`push now` is the same drain the app runs on open and on focus, so the panel adds no second way
to sync. `discard all` is the one control in Mine that can lose work, so it confirms through the
browser's own prompt, the way *forget this device* does on the tile screen, rather than through
the calendar's discard prompt — whose **don't ask again** would switch this guard off along with
the one it belongs to. Discarding also forgets the local copy of every path it held and drops the
ETag, so the next pull restores exactly what GitHub holds; forgetting the queue alone would leave
text in the mirror that no later pull would ever reconcile.

**The sync line is a button.** It is what you are looking at when you want to know why it says
what it says, and reaching the panel through the hamburger only helps once you know the panel is
there.

| overlay | holds |
| --- | --- |
| Filter (a dropdown) | a **Category** row, a **Stage** row and **important only**; on the board also an **assignee** |
| Settings (a centred panel) | the nine rows below |
| Logs (a centred panel) | the last sync attempt, the changes still queued, `push now`, `discard all` |

**The stages and importance narrow every view, not only the board.** The stage list holds a
checkbox per stage — `Todo`, `Doing`, `Done`, each with its colour. A month with the done ones out of it is as much a thing to want as a board of them.

A stage switched off hides **tasks** and nothing else: an event has no stage to be judged by.
`important only` hides whatever is not marked, **events included**, because that is what the
words say and a month of what matters is the thing worth having. Both are remembered per device,
like the groups: a filter that empties a month is one you want to find still on after a reload —
and the filter button says it is.

**A filter that is on says so on its button**: a small count at its top right, in a circle.
It counts **one per kind of narrowing** — the groups, the stages, importance, the assignee — so
it never passes four. One per switched-off thing would read `16` in a repo with twenty groups

**The categories and stages are each behind a row** — an icon with `Category` or `Stage` beside it — so the filter stays short however many

| row | control |

# Calendar — technical requirements

File format and rendering for [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md). Sync, caching and writes are

## Paths

```

calendar/2026/04/2026-04-25-0000-ov1q.md     occurrence override
```

humans: the repo browses chronologically on github.com, and no directory grows past a month of
entries. `-k3f9` is 4 random characters, **not** a counter — two devices creating entries offline

or an override the two can disagree. Always read `start`. Changing an entry's date is a rename,
which is a delete plus a create in one commit.

open-ended rule must render in months it was not created in and there is no month folder to find
it under.

| `title` | both | required |
| `type` | both | `event` or `task` |
| `start` | both | `DTSTART`. A bare date (`2026-04-18`) is all-day; a timestamp (`2026-04-18T14:00:00Z`) is an instant |
| `end` | both | same value types as `start`; omitted when a single all-day item. **Inclusive**: an all-day `end` is the last day, not the day after |
| `group` | both | a name, resolved through `groups.md` |
| `stage` | `task` only | `todo` / `doing` / `done` |
| `important` | both | `true` when important; absent otherwise, never `false`. Ours, no RFC 5545 equivalent |
| `location` | both | free text |
| `alerts` | both | minutes before start, `0` = at start. Stored and exported only; nothing fires in the background |
| `participants` | both | list of email addresses |
| `recurrence` | both | RRULE string, e.g. `FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA` |
| `exdate` / `rdate` | recurring | occurrences to skip / extra occurrences |
| `status` | override | `cancelled` removes the occurrence. The only value used |
| `series` | override | id of the recurring file it belongs to |
| `recurrence-id` | override | the original occurrence date this file replaces |
| `conflictOf` | conflict file | written by sync |

No `duration` key — it is `end - start`.

`end` is **inclusive**, which is the one place the format departs from RFC 5545: there an
all-day `DTEND` is exclusive, so a Monday-to-Wednesday trip ends on the Thursday. Here it ends on
the Wednesday — the file says what the popup asked for and what a person reading the repo by hand
would mean — and an `.ics` export is the place that adds the day back. A timed `end` at midnight
is read as the end of the day before, so `22:00`–`00:00` covers one evening rather than two days.

An occurrence therefore carries two day keys: `dayKey`, the day it starts, and `endDayKey`, the
last day it covers. The range query is an **overlap** — `dayKey <= to && endDayKey >= from` —
rather than a test of where it starts, and a recurring entry's rule is expanded over a window
widened by the length of one occurrence, or an occurrence that began before the range would
never be generated at all.

There is no `priority` key. It was RFC 5545 `PRIORITY` and a scale of 1 to 3; importance is a
yes or no, so the scale had nothing to say. A file carrying one is not read for it, and the key
goes the next time the entry is saved, along with anything else the form does not own.

Type and time are independent: `type` decides whether the entry has a stage - `important` is
not a task's any more - and the value type of `start` decides whether it is all-day or timed. A task is usually all-day, but may carry a time
and then renders at it.

There is no `estimate` key either. It was a task's size in days, it was never read by anything
but its own field, and a number nobody acted on is a field that only asks to be filled in. A
file carrying one is not read for it — and unlike `priority`, **it is not taken out on the next
save**: the form does not own the key any more, so it survives untouched like any other key the
form never wrote, and the only thing that removes it is a hand that opens the file.

`stage` is a task's only progress field; there is no `done` key. A `stage` that is absent or is
not one of the three reads as `todo`.

`status` is deliberately *not* the stage field. It already means cancellation on an override,
and one key cannot carry both without an override's cancellation reading as a kanban column.

The bare-date form matters. An all-day task stored as `2026-04-18T00:00:00Z` lands on the wrong
day outside UTC and shifts twice a year on DST.

The markdown body is the entry's content and is preserved byte-for-byte by anything that does not
explicitly edit it.

The apps in the subfolders are pages inside it, not separate installs. This is what makes the central requirement work: **the GitHub repo and token are entered once, in the main app, and every app in a subfolder uses them.** Verified on iPhone and Android. ## Main app A tile per app: its `icon.svg` above its folder name. ## First run 1. Open the app URL and add it to the home screen (iOS: Share → Add to Home Screen; Android: menu → Install). 2. The setup screen asks for GitHub owner, data repo, branch, and a personal access token. 3. The app tests the connection and reports clearly if it fails. Settings are stored on the device only. That is what makes an overlay read as lifted, so none of them needs a heavy border or a dark drop shadow. **Dark** is a deep navy with paper-coloured ink and an amber accent. "System" follows the device between these two. Two more can be chosen, and choosing one pins it day and night: **coffee**, an espresso near-black with surfaces stepped clearly above it, paper-coloured ink and an ember accent, and **neutral**, the warm off-white Linen with a terracotta accent and no grey anywhere in it. Both are **glyphs on no background**: a save is a green disk, a trashcan is a red trashcan. **Nothing in Mine is a filled green button.** The weight of a primary action comes from the icon being the familiar one in the familiar place, not from a block of colour — and a save drawn like the rest of the row cannot be mistaken for a background that means something. The way out of an overlay is in the same corner wherever you are, so leaving one is never something to look for — and that corner is worth more to the button reached for by habit than to the one aimed at deliberately. Two renderers would drift, and a note that looked right in one app and wrong in the next would be the plainest possible sign that these files are not as portable as the whole idea claims. ## Entry popup

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so do
the settings panel and the day preview. Nothing rises from the bottom edge any more. A centred
card is reached with either thumb and does not pretend to be a drawer that can be dragged. The
hamburger's menu and the filter hang off their buttons instead, as dropdowns, and a field's own
popup hangs off its row; those three name the thing they came from, which a centred card cannot.

**There is one popup, and it is both.** Clicking an entry — in any grid, in the day preview, or
as a card on the board — opens the entry, shown as text, and **every value in it is edited where
it is read**: click the thing, change it, and one save at the top writes the lot. There is no
pen, no second popup behind one, and no mode to be in.

It was two before, a read-only preview with a pen into a form, and the reason was sound: a form
answers *what day is this on* in input boxes, which are harder to read than text and leave every
value one slip away from a tap meant to scroll. Editing in place keeps that — a row is text until
it is clicked, so there is still nothing to slip into — and gives back the two things the split
cost. A change was four taps before the field was even typed into: open, pen, row, and back. And
the preview and the
form had to agree about every field twice over, in two blocks of code, which is how one of them
came to show the stage and the other to hide it.

**Each row is edited in place, and one save writes.** The rows hold a draft; nothing reaches the
repo until the popup's own disk, so **one entry edit is one commit** and the popup is one
transaction rather than a stream of them. A row that writes the file the moment it is saved was
tried on paper and gives this popup three faults it cannot see: the entry it is holding goes a
generation stale after the first write, a saved date moves the file out from under it, and four
rows saved offline queue four writes to one path. One save at the end has none of them.

**The disk appears only once something differs from the file**, and it is the only button in the
popup that writes. A popup opened to read has no save in it to wonder about — which is most
openings — and a save that is there is a save with something to do.

```
[☑]                                  [trash] [x]      opened, nothing changed
[☑]                          [trash] [disk] [x]       a row has been changed
[☑] [📅]                             [disk] [x]       a new one: the type is still a choice,
                                                      and the disk is disabled until it has a title
[☑] [this|all]               [trash] [disk] [x]       a repeating one: the scope pair
```

The top row carries **the type**, then right-aligned a trashcan to delete the entry, the disk
once there is something to save, and an `x` to close. On an entry that already exists the type is
a **marker, not a choice** — a ticked square for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and
not pressable — because a task turned into an event drops its stage, its importance and its
importance, and the type is settled when the entry is made. On a new entry it is the pair, with the
event selected. On a repeating one the **scope pair** follows the marker, left of the gap —
described below.

The trashcan stays at the left of that group: deleting is not an edit of a field, it writes at
once whatever the draft holds, and the board's rule that a card is deleted from its popup in two
taps depends on the trashcan being on the first of them.

Below the row, in this order: the **title**, the **when**, the **toggle row**, the **five field
rows**, and the **details body** last. Nothing about repeating is among them.

### A row, and a row being edited

Every row is **the icon, then the value** — no field name beside it:

```
[ball]    Work                                      [trash]
[pin]     Conference room 3B                        [trash]
[repeat]  Repeat
[bell]    Alerts
```

The name is gone because it said the same thing as the icon it sat beside, in the one column
where the value has to fit. **An unset row shows the field's name in its place, muted** — which
is what an empty input does everywhere else in Mine, and what keeps a bell from being a bell and
### The details body

Last in the popup, and **shown in full and rendered** — not clipped to two lines, not as raw
markdown — by [Mine's shared renderer](../REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies). Two lines on a card
and the whole text here are the difference between a glance and having opened the thing, and that
is the one thing the old preview existed for, so it is not spent on making the body look like the
rows above it.

It carries a small header of its own: the `lines` icon, and the trashcan at the right when there
is a body to clear. **Clicking the body makes it active**, replacing the rendered text with the
raw markdown in a textarea and putting the `x` in that same header beside the trashcan. A body
is read far more often than it is written, which is the same argument the rows make, with more
text behind it — and the body's header is the shape every open row takes, since a textarea is
the clearest case for why the buttons do not sit under the editor.

### A new entry

A new entry is **a draft like any other edit**, and no row behaves differently in it. It opens
with its title row active and the when seeded from wherever it was made — the cell, the day
preview's `+`, or a kanban column header, which seeds the stage as well — and every other row is
live from the start. The disk creates the file; until it is pressed, a `+` opened and thought
better of leaves no file and no commit.

**The disk is disabled until the title has something in it**, because an entry must have one.
That is the only way a new entry differs from an edit of a saved one, and it is a disabled button
rather than a rule about which row may be touched first.

### A repeating entry

A repeating entry carries one thing the rest do not: **the scope pair**, `this` or `all`, in the
top row immediately right of the type marker. It governs **what the two writes in that row do** —
the disk and the trashcan both — and it is one choice about one write, which is what it always
was. Switching it rebuilds the draft from the other file, so it also resets what a discard is
measured against.

It sits in the top row because that is where the controls it governs are. Below the title it
needed a line saying *Part of a repeating entry* to explain itself; beside the marker, between
the type and the trashcan, it explains itself, and that line is gone with it.

**It reads `this` and `all`, not the noun.** The entry behind it is a task as often as an event,
and the marker a thumb's width to its left already says which; a pair reading *all events* above
a ticked square would be wrong on half the entries that have one. Two words also fit a top row
that already holds a marker, a trashcan, a disk and an `x` without wrapping on a phone.

**There is no `skip this one`.** Skipping one occurrence is what the trashcan does when the pair
says `this` — a delete scoped the same way a save is, by the same control, rather than a link
that did one of the two things on the row by another name. With `all` the trashcan deletes the
whole entry, which is what it always did. Both ask first.

Only the series carries the rule, so **the repetition row is absent on an occurrence override** —
a rule the popup must not rewrite has no row at all.

### Saving, and leaving

The disk **closes the popup and returns to the calendar immediately**; the push to GitHub runs in
the background and is reported in the sync line, not in the popup. **Both ways out land on the
calendar**, the disk and the `x` alike. The cell or the card behind it shows the result anyway,
and there is no preview left to step back to.

Deleting the entry, by either scope, also closes the popup, because it leaves nothing to look
at.

### Discarding an edit

**Leaving a popup that holds unsaved changes asks first.** The popup's `x`, a click on the
backdrop and Escape are one way out and ask one question: a small centred prompt offering
**discard** or **keep editing**. A popup that has not been touched closes without a word — the
question is about losing work, and there is none to lose, which is also when there is no disk in
the top row to have missed. A half-written new entry counts as work: it is as easy to lose as an
edit of a saved one, and one rule covering both is shorter than two with an exception between
them.

**A row's own `x` is not guarded**, and has nothing to guard: it closes a row and keeps what is
in it. Nothing is lost by pressing it, which is the whole reason it is not the one that asks.

The prompt carries a **don't ask again** toggle. Ticking it silences the prompt on that device for
good, so the `x` goes straight back to discarding. That is a preference about this screen's
behaviour rather than data, so it is stored on the device like the rest of them — and it has a
row in the panel's settings section, because nothing in Mine may be switched off from a place
that cannot switch it back on.

What the merge changes about losing work is only where it is typed. The unit is still the whole
popup, the question is still asked once, and the disk is still the one thing that writes — so an
entry is never half-written to the repo, and a row left open when the disk is pressed is taken
along with the rest.

# Mine — technical requirements

How [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) is built. Everything here was verified against the live
API or on device on 2026-11-19; the device checks were
run by a throwaway page since removed — see [Platform findings](#platform-findings).

## Repos

| Repo | Visibility | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maximilianharr/mine` | public | this app, served by Pages at `/mine/` |
| `maximilianharr/mine-data` | **private** | the markdown data |

Pages cannot serve a private repo without Enterprise, so data in the app repo would be
world-readable at a predictable URL. The token is scoped to the data repo only.

## Layout

One `manifest.json` with `scope: /mine/`, one service worker at the root. Subfolders are ordinary
pages inside that scope. `/mine/` and `/mine/calendar/` are the same origin, so they share one
IndexedDB — that is the whole mechanism behind "enter the token once".

```
/index.html /manifest.json /sw.js
/style.css  the shared base      /home.css  the tile screen's own
/shared/  apps.js  store.js  github.js  md.js  markdown.js  prefs.js
          ui.js  sync.js  search.js  vendor/
/calendar/  index.html  app.js  data.js  ui.js  views.js  kanban.js  popup.js  settings.js
            style.css  icon.svg  sample/
/test/    run.sh  unit.mjs  serve.py  cdp.mjs  check-mine.mjs  check-calendar.mjs
```

No build step: no bundler, no CI, no node_modules. `git push` deploys, every page opens from
disk, all paths relative so the `/mine/` prefix needs no config.

The checks in `test/` hold to the same rule: `run.sh` drives a headless Chromium over the
DevTools protocol with nothing installed, and what it covers — and the two mistakes that make
it lie to you — are in [TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md). One browser suite per app,
`check-<slug>.mjs`, discovered by `run.sh` rather than listed in it, over the harness in
`cdp.mjs`.

`shared/ui.js` is the chrome every app builds its screens out of: the DOM helpers, the icon set,
the three overlay mechanisms and the settings row. `shared/sync.js` is the sync line and the logs
panel. Both exist because both apps had their own copy: the drain-then-pull sequence was written
twice, the icon set and the overlays sat in `calendar/ui.js`, and the logs panel - which reports
on a queue shared by every app - was reachable only from the calendar.

Two couplings were cut to get them out of the calendar. `closePops()` took its list of overlays
from a literal naming the calendar's; it now takes it from `registerPops()`, which an app calls
once at boot, and the `aria-expanded` it resets is tracked by `openPop()` rather than named. The
icon set is shared for the verbs and the two conventions REQUIREMENTS.md states for all of Mine -
a green disk saves, a red trashcan deletes - and an app merges its own subjects in with
`addIcons()`; a second app drawing its own trashcan is how those conventions would quietly stop
being conventions.

`shared/search.js` is the search every app opens over its own folder. It reads the mirror with
`allFiles(folder)` and nothing else, so it is offline by construction, and it is given its
format rather than knowing one: `openSearch({ folder, title, date, fields, open })` names the
folder, the frontmatter keys for the title and the date, the further keys to search, and what a
result does when pressed. Its matching - `index()`, `find()`, `snippet()` - is pure and checked in
`test/unit.mjs`; the popup it builds itself and appends to the page, as `#search-pop`, so an app
needs no markup for it, only that id in its `registerPops()` list so its scrim and Escape close
it. Opening it re-reads the folder; `refreshSearch()`, called from an app's render, re-reads it
while it is open, so a result edited from the search reads as saved. The index is rebuilt on
every open rather than kept: a few thousand small files parse in milliseconds, and a kept index
is a second copy of the mirror that can disagree with it.

`shared/apps.js` exports the app list and is imported by the tile screen, `sw.js` and
`github.js`, so adding an app means editing one array, and its `files` are what the worker
precaches. The list is
written by hand on purpose: `install` uses `cache.addAll`, which rejects as a whole if any URL
404s, so a wrong entry fails loudly at install. A *missing* one fails silently, which is how
`shared/markdown.js` stayed out of the shell while `popup.js` imported it — an app installed and
taken offline before an entry was ever opened could not draw a details body.

1. **`/<slug>/`** with `index.html`, `icon.svg`, your modules, and `style.css` if it needs one.

## Stylesheets

`style.css` is the **shared base**: the tokens, the form primitives, and the chrome every app
builds its screens out of - the icon button, the three overlay mechanisms, the settings row, the
logs panel and a rendered markdown body. Each app's own stylesheet loads after it and holds only
what is its own.

Every token is declared three times - once for the light theme, once inside the
`prefers-color-scheme: dark` query for the device's own choice, and once under
`:root[data-theme="dark"]` for the setting that overrides it - and that pair carry the same
values. The chosen palettes, `coffee` and `neutral`, are declared once each under
their own `data-theme`, after that pair, which they beat at equal specificity by coming
later. `applyTheme` also sets the `theme-color` metas to the pinned theme's `--bg`, and gives
them back their own media-keyed values for `system`. Beyond the colours themselves the set holds `--raise`, the surface a popup or a card
sits on, one shade above `--bg`; `--chip-bg`, the mix an entry's own
colour is drawn with, which differs between the themes because a dark page needs more tint; and `--serif` / `--sans` / `--mono`, so no stylesheet names a font family of its
own. **There are no web fonts**: the CSP is `default-src 'self'`, so every stack is system fonts
with a metric-compatible fallback behind the first name.

A colour that has to hold in both themes cannot be written in JavaScript, because the code
cannot see which theme is on. The calendar's three stage colours are the case: `STAGE_COLOR`
hands out `var(--todo)` rather than a hex, and an inline `style.color = 'var(--todo)'` resolves
against whichever theme is live. A colour that comes from the user's own data - a category's -
can only be the one hex they wrote, so the stylesheet mixes it against the theme instead: the
app sets `--c` on the element and the two `--chip-*` mixes do the rest.

`home.css` is the tile screen's own, loaded by the root `index.html` alone. It is there because
the tile screen is one app among the others: a full-width filled button and a 44rem body are its
choices, and while they sat in the base every app page had to undo them.

A rule in the base is a rule an app can no longer forget. `[hidden] { display: none !important }`
is the clearest case - a class rule setting `display` beats the UA stylesheet's `[hidden]`, so a
screen or a banner renders while still carrying the attribute. The calendar carried that rule and
the tile screen did not, which is why the root app showed "Update ready - reload" permanently.
The `.md-*` rules are the second case: `shared/markdown.js` is one renderer for every app, and
its stylesheet has to be shared with it or the second app renders a body unstyled.

Moving `.ib` into the base changed one thing on purpose. The kanban's `.knav` and `.kadd` carry
`.ib` and declare their own sizes; `.ib` used to come later in the same sheet and win, so those
sizes were dead. They apply now, which is what they were written to do.

`shared/md.js` and `shared/markdown.js` are two different jobs and stay two files. `md.js` is the
file envelope — it parses and serialises frontmatter and is imported by the paths that read and
write the repo. `markdown.js` renders a body for the screen and is imported only by UI, so nothing
on the file-IO path pulls a renderer in. It **returns a DOM node and never a string of HTML**, which
is what makes a body carrying a `<script>` tag harmless without a sanitiser to get right; what it
covers and why it is hand-rolled rather than vendored is in
[REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies).

## Modules

```
calendar/data.js      the model, the date and sprint arithmetic, and the writes
calendar/ui.js        DOM helpers, the icon set, and the state every view reads
calendar/views.js     year, month, week, day, and the day preview
calendar/kanban.js    the board
calendar/drag.js      press-and-drag, for a card, an entry and the top pane
calendar/popup.js     the one entry popup: its rows, their inline editors, their writes
calendar/settings.js  the filter dropdown, the settings panel and the logs panel: the filter

calendar/app.js       the top pane, navigation, the picker, the zoom, the menu, the search's

```

`ui.js` holds the state in one object with `render`, `status`, `push`, `refresh` and `reload` as
slots the shell fills in, so a view can ask for a redraw or a background push without importing
`app.js` back and making an import cycle. The logs panel's `push now` goes through `refresh`,
which is the same serialised drain-then-pull the app runs on open and on focus.

**Dragging is pointer events, in `drag.js`**, not HTML5 drag and drop, which never fires for a
finger. `draggable(host, { item, target, drop, start, end })` listens for a press on the host;
`item` says what the press picks up and `target(x, y)` what lies under a point, read with
`elementFromPoint` while the lifted copy has `pointer-events: none`. A touch lifts after a 400 ms
hold with less than 8 px of movement, and anything more is left to the browser as a scroll; a
mouse lifts after 5 px. Once lifted, a non-passive `touchmove` listener on the window cancels the
page's own scrolling — it is registered once, at load, because a listener added mid-gesture is
too late on iOS — and the scroller under the item is scrolled by the pointer's distance into its
48 px edge. The first click within 400 ms of a release is swallowed, so a drop is never also a
click on whatever it landed on. A held element carries `user-select: none` and
`-webkit-touch-callout: none`, or iOS raises its callout instead.

**The pane is docked by a class on `body`**, `dock-bottom`, read from `calendar.barPosition` in
the KV store at boot and set by a drop. The stylesheet does the rest by `order` inside `#cal`'s
column — the sync line first, the view, the pane last and sticky at `bottom: 0` — and on a phone
gives the period row `order: 0` so the buttons are the lower row. The dropdowns need nothing:
`openPop` already flips a dropdown above its button when there is no room below. The pane is
`draggable` with `hold: 'always'`, so a mouse must hold too: every pixel of the pane is a button,
and a slightly sloppy click must not move it.

`FIELDS` in `popup.js` is built while the module is still evaluating, so anything it calls must
be a function *declaration* — a `const` arrow is still in its temporal dead zone at that point.

**There are three overlay mechanisms.** `openPop` positions a dropdown under the button that
opened it — the date picker, the zoom, the hamburger's menu and the filter. The search, which is
`shared/search.js`'s, is a `.pop` hung from the top of the screen and opened with `openCentred`'s
scrim. `openCentred` only
unhides something already placed by `.centred` — the settings panel, the day preview, the group
manager. `openRowPop` is the third, and the one thing that distinguishes it is what it does *not*
do: it raises **no scrim**. That is deliberate and it is the reason it cannot be one of the other
two. A field's popup is dismissed by a tap that must still reach whatever it landed on, so that
moving from one field to the next is one tap; a scrim would stop that tap, and two taps to change
field is the friction this whole shape exists to remove. The filter's category and stage lists
open the same way, over the filter, whose scrim already covers them. `justClosed` in `popup.js` is the other
half of it: the capture-phase click listener closes the popup *before* the row's own handler runs,
so without it the tap that closed a popup would immediately reopen it.

Both `openPop` and `openRowPop` place through one `place()` in `ui.js`, which flips the popup above
its anchor when there is no room below — a field row near the foot of a long entry popup is the
case that needs it.

`openFieldPop` looks its anchor up by `data-field` rather than taking the node. On a dismissing
tap the capture-phase listener re-renders the rows before the row's own handler runs, so by the
time that handler asks for a popup its node is detached and its `getBoundingClientRect()` is all
zeros. The handler itself still fires: a click's propagation path is computed at dispatch, so
detaching the target mid-dispatch does not cancel it.

The popup-over-a-popup layer — `#sub` and `#sub-scrim` — is no longer part of editing an entry.
It survives for the group manager alone, which is reached from the settings panel and edits no
entry, and so is still the one overlay below the top row's disk that writes.

The one popup means one builder. There is no `viewCard` beside `fillForm` any more: a row is
drawn from the same `FIELDS` entry whether it is showing a value or editing one, which is what
stops the two from disagreeing about a field — the preview showing the stage while the form hid
it was exactly that, in two functions that had to be kept in step by hand. `mode` on a `FIELDS`
entry is the whole of how a field is edited: `inline` puts its control in the row, `pop` in a
popup anchored to the row, `block` is the body.

**A row's height is held by CSS, not by what it contains.** `.frow` carries a `min-height` set by
the tallest thing a row can hold — its trashcan and its `x`, which a set row already carries shut
— and every control a row opens is shorter than that. Nothing in script measures or equalises
anything, so a row cannot change height by being opened.

A mechanism invented twice is how the day preview came to be anchored by script and then dragged
back to the middle with `left: 50% !important` — one rule undoing another, in two files.

Every icon comes from the one table in `ui.js`. The buttons in `index.html` are empty and are
filled by `icon()` at boot, so an icon cannot drift between a hand-written path in the markup and
the table the views draw from.

## Width

`#cal` carries **no `max-width`**: the pane, the calendar window and the sync line are as wide as
the browser. The cap lives on the board alone — `.view.vK .kb` is `max-width: 78rem` and
`margin-inline: auto`, in both orientations — so the pane cannot change width when the view does.
A cap put back on `#cal` for the board's sake is the mistake this split exists to prevent: it
narrows the pane with it, and the pane then jumps every time the board icon is pressed.

The year grid is capped at six columns rather than by a container width, with
`repeat(auto-fill, minmax(max(10.5rem, (100% - 5 * .7rem) / 6), 1fr))` against its `gap: .7rem`.
The `max()` is what stops `auto-fill` from adding a seventh track on a wide monitor while still
letting the grid reflow to four, three and two as it narrows. **The five gaps have to be
subtracted**: a bare `100% / 6` makes six tracks plus five gaps wider than the container, so
`auto-fill` fits five and a year reads as 5 + 5 + 2 — the opposite of the fix.

## Service worker version

The update banner compares versions rather than merely noticing a waiting worker. The worker
answers a `version` message with its `VERSION` constant; the UI shows "Update ready" only when a
waiting worker's version differs from the active one's. `reg.waiting` alone is not the condition
— a byte-identical worker can wait, and then the banner never goes away.
### Moving the pane to the bottom

**The pane can be dragged to the bottom of the screen, and back.** Pressing anywhere on it for a
moment — a button included, with a finger or a mouse — lifts the whole pane, both rows on a
phone; two dashed places appear at the top and the bottom of the screen, the one in whose half
the pane is held is marked, and releasing docks it there. A press that does not hold is still a
click on whatever was pressed, and a hold opens nothing. Where it is docked is **remembered per
device**, like the board's orientation, and holds for every view, the board included.

At the bottom, **the sync line moves to the top**, so the two never stack, and **on a phone the
two rows swap**: the period goes on the upper row and the six buttons on the lower, nearest the
thumb. The pane keeps clear of the home indicator. The dropdowns it opens — the zoom, the
picker, the filter, the menu — **open upwards**, as any dropdown does that has no room below its
button. The search still hangs from the top of the screen, where the keyboard does not cover it.

### The zoom

A button beside the view switch, opening a short list under itself. **It draws the view you are
in rather than an icon of its own**: in a calendar view the letter of the period — `D`, `W`, `M`
or `Y` — and on the board the orientation, three columns side by side or three bands stacked.
No single drawing says "change the view" without also looking like one of the views, and a
button that names where you are tells you that and where to tap in one. The bands are filled
bars rather than lines, so the stacked one cannot be read as the hamburger.

**The list offers what the view it was opened in can do, and nothing else:**

| view | the list |

# Notes

Notes is an app of [Mine](../REQUIREMENTS.md) for quick notes, in the spirit of Google Keep. Every
note is one markdown file in the data repo, so your notes stay readable and portable without this
app.

See [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) for the file format.

## What a note holds

A **title**, **tags**, and a free markdown **body**. The file also records when the note was
created and when it was last updated; neither is edited by hand in the app.

**The title is required**, as a calendar entry's is: every card and every search result has a
name to be found by.

**Tags are plain words**, as many as you like, in lower case, a space becoming `-`. They have no
colour and no file of their own: a tag exists as long as some note carries it, and the list of
tags anywhere in the app is the list the notes carry.

There is nothing else — no pin, no archive, no colour, no reminder. A deleted note is deleted;
the repo's history is the archive. Each of these is one frontmatter key away if it is ever
wanted.

## Layout

The header at the top, and a grid of cards below it, **the most recently updated first**.

```
[+] [search]                       [filter] [☰] [⌂]
```

The header is **one row at every width**, a phone at 320 px included: the five buttons are the
calendar's own, drawn the same size, and there is no period to need a second row. On a phone the
five share the width equally.

- **`+`** opens a new note. Notes have no cell to create one in, so the header carries it.
- **search** opens Mine's search over `notes/`.
- **filter** opens the filter, a dropdown off its button.
- **☰** names `settings` and `logs`, and opens whichever is tapped.
- **⌂** goes back to the Mine tile screen.

**The header can be dragged to the bottom of the screen, and back**, exactly as the calendar's
pane: hold it for a moment, a button included, drag it into the other half and release. At the
bottom the sync line moves to the top. Where it is docked is **one setting for all of Mine**: dock
it at the bottom in the calendar and it is at the bottom here too.

The sync line sits below the cards, or above them when the header is docked at the bottom, and is
a button to the logs, as in the calendar.

## The cards

A card shows the **title** in the serif, then the **body rendered** by [Mine's shared
renderer](../REQUIREMENTS.md#markdown-bodies) and cut off after about eight lines, then the
**tags** as `#home #shopping`, and the **updated date** in Mine's date format. A note with an
empty body is a title, its tags and its date.

**One column on a phone, more as the screen widens** — two, three, four — each column a stack of
cards of their own heights, as Keep lays them out. The order runs down the first column and then
the next, which is what CSS columns do; reading order across the top row is not kept, and a grid
of notes is scanned rather than read in sequence.

Tapping a card opens the note. A checkbox on a card is drawn, not operated, as everywhere in
Mine.

With nothing to show, the grid says so: `No notes yet — + makes one`, or, with a filter on,
`No notes match the filter`.

## The note popup

**The calendar's popup, with fewer rows.** A note opens in the middle of the screen, shown as text
and rendered, and **every value is edited where it is read**: tap the title and it is a text box,
tap the body and it is a textarea of raw markdown. There is no pen and no mode.

```
                                     [trash] [x]      opened, nothing changed
                             [trash] [disk] [x]       something has been changed
                                     [disk] [x]       a new one; the disk is disabled until it has a title
```

Below the top row: the **title**, the **tags row**, and the **body** last.

- **The disk appears only once something differs from the file**, and it is the only thing that
  writes. One save is one commit, and it sets `updated`. The disk closes the popup.
- **The trashcan** asks the browser's own confirm, then deletes the file and closes the popup.
- **The `x`**, a tap on the backdrop and Escape close it. With unsaved changes they ask first —
  **discard** or **keep editing**, with a **don't ask again** — the calendar's prompt, and the same
  setting: ticking *don't ask again* in either app silences it in both, and the settings row in
  either turns it back on.

**The tags row** reads `#home #shopping`, or a muted `Tags` when there are none. Tapping it opens
a small popup off the row with a checkbox for every tag any note carries — this note's ticked —
and a box to type a new one, which is added and ticked on Enter. Unticking a tag removes it from
this note only.

**The body** is shown in full and rendered. Tapping it replaces it with the raw markdown in a
textarea; the textarea grows with its text.

**A new note** opens empty with the title active, so the keyboard is up at once. Nothing is
written until the disk; a `+` thought better of leaves no file. A new note opened with a filter
on starts with the filter's tags ticked, so it lands in the grid you are looking at.

## Search

The magnifier opens Mine's search over `notes/` and nothing else. A note's title, body and tags
are searched, and a result is dated by its `updated`. A result opens the note **over** the
search; closing it comes back to the search as it was. Search ignores the filter.

## The filter, the settings and the logs

**The filter** is a dropdown off the funnel with a checkbox per tag, alphabetically, and
`untagged` last. **With nothing ticked every note shows.** Ticking tags narrows the grid to the
notes that carry **any** of them — `#home` and `#work` together show both — and `untagged` adds
the notes with no tag. It is the reverse of the calendar's filter, where everything starts ticked:
with dozens of tags, "show me these" is the common case and "hide those" is not.

It is remembered per device, and **a filter that is on says so on its button**: the number of
ticked tags, in a small circle at its top right. A tag that no note carries any more drops out of
the filter by itself.

**The settings** are a centred panel with three rows, all of them Mine-wide:

| row | control |
| --- | --- |
| Theme | system, light, dark, coffee or neutral |
| Date format | `auto`, `dd.mm.yyyy` or `mm/dd/yy` |
| Confirm discard | whether leaving an edited popup asks first |

**The logs** are Mine's shared logs panel, as in the calendar.

## On a phone

Every screen fits a 320 CSS px viewport, light and dark, and nothing moves sideways. The cards
are one column; the popup and the panels are centred cards, as in the calendar.

# Notes — technical requirements

File format for [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md). Sync, caching and writes are in
[../TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](../TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md).

## Paths

```
notes/2026/11/2026-11-26-1430-k3f9.md
```

The calendar's scheme, keyed on the **creation** time in UTC: the repo browses chronologically on
github.com and no folder grows past a month. `-k3f9` is 4 random characters, so two devices
creating notes offline in the same minute never mint the same name. No title slug, so retitling
is never a rename — **the path never changes** after creation. Every `.md` under `notes/` is a
note; there is no settings or tags file.

## Frontmatter

```
---
title: Groceries
created: 2026-11-26T14:30:00Z
updated: 2026-11-26T15:02:11Z
tags:
  - home
  - shopping
---
```

| Key | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `title` | required by the app |
| `created` | UTC instant to the second, set once when the note is first saved |
| `updated` | UTC instant to the second, set by every save from the app |
| `tags` | a YAML list, lower case, a space written as `-`; omitted when empty |

Written by `shared/md.js`'s `serialize`, so empty keys are omitted, never `None`. **A key the app
does not own survives a save**, and the body is preserved byte-for-byte by anything that does not
edit it.

A file written by hand is read leniently. A missing `updated` falls back to `created`, then to
the date in the path; a missing `title` shows the first `#` heading or the file name; a `tags`
given as a single string is one tag. The grid sorts on `updated`, newest first, with the path as
the tie-break.

## Modules

```
notes/app.js     the whole app: the model, the grid, the popup, the filter, the settings, boot
notes/style.css  the grid, the cards and the popup's rows
```

One module: the app is a fraction of the calendar, and a split into model and views would be
files that import only each other. The model is `buildNotes(files)` — the mirror's `notes/`
files parsed and sorted — and is exported for `test/unit.mjs`.

Everything else is shared: the store and the sync (`shared/store.js`, `github.js`, `sync.js`),
the renderer, the search, the prefs, the icon set and overlays (`shared/ui.js`), and the header
drag (`shared/drag.js`, `dockable()` in `shared/ui.js`). The discard prompt reads and writes
`mine.confirmDiscard`; the dock position is `mine.barPosition`. The filter is `notes.tags` in
`kv`, the ticked tags as a list, `''` standing for `untagged`.

The popup holds a **draft** — title, tags, body — and compares it with the note as opened; the
disk shows when the two differ. A save rewrites the frontmatter it read with the draft's three
fields and a new `updated`, leaving every other key as it was.

## Service worker

`notes` is one entry in `shared/apps.js`, and its files are precached like the calendar's.

A set of small PWAs that keep your personal data as markdown in a private GitHub repo —
calendar, zettelkasten, diary — so it stays portable and free of vendor lock-in.

**Live: https://maximilianharr.github.io/mine/** — install it to your home screen.

## Docs

| | |
| --- | --- |
| [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) | what the app does and how it behaves |
| [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) | how it is built, and the verified platform findings |
| [TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md) | what is checked before a change ships, and how |
| [calendar/](calendar/) | the calendar app, with its own pair of docs |
| [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) | how to find your way around without reading all of it |

## Layout

```
style.css                                         the shared base: tokens and chrome
index.html app.js home.css sw.js manifest.json    the main app
shared/   apps.js store.js github.js md.js        used by every app
          markdown.js prefs.js ui.js sync.js
          vendor/
calendar/                                         one folder per app
test/                                             the checks: test/run.sh
```

No build step: no bundler, no CI, no dependencies to install. `git push` deploys to GitHub
Pages. To run it locally, `python3 -m http.server` in this folder and open the printed URL.
`test/run.sh` runs the model checks in node and the rest in a headless browser, and installs
nothing either.

Data lives in a **separate private repo**, never in this one. The token is entered once in the
app, stored on the device, and scoped so it can only touch that data repo.

## Status

The main app, the sync layer and the on-device checks are done and verified end to end against a
real repo. The calendar is built — the five views, the kanban, the entry popup and its field
popups, the filter and the settings — and `test/run.sh` covers it.

## A check must be able to fail

Before trusting a new check, break the thing it covers and watch it go red. A fit check written
against `--window-size` passes on a broken layout; a colour check that names `#0a7b3e` instead
of resolving `--good` passes when the token changes underneath it. Removing `min-width: 0` from
`.day` must turn the month fit checks red, and putting it back must turn them green.

## What the harness cannot tell you

Headless Chromium on a desktop is not a phone. It does not cover:

- **the real device** — a system font scale, a notch, a software keyboard, Safari's and
  Chrome's own quirks. Serve the tree with `python3 -m http.server` and open it from the phone
  on the same network, or push and open the live URL.
- **installing to the home screen, the service worker and the update banner** — these need an
  installed app over HTTPS. The platform questions are answered in
  [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md#platform-findings).
- **GitHub sync**: pulling, the one-commit drain, conflict files, an expiring token. Only a real
  token against the real data repo exercises those, and that is done by hand.

A change to any of those three is checked on a device before it ships, and
[TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) records what was found and when.
